subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 45 minutes × 16 periods = 720 minutes
Total: 16 periods · 12h 0min

periods.activity_title: Mean as a Balance Point on the Number Line

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 5.1 p.113
textbook_items_in_class.description: A dot plot shows a collection with its mean of 9 but one dot is missing; mark the missing value to restore the balance.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 5.1 p.114
textbook_items_in_class.description: Three dot plots show song lengths for different albums; identify which has a mean of 5.57 minutes and explain the reasoning.

time_bands.activity: Open by asking students to place the numbers 2, 4, and 9 on a hand-drawn number line and guess where the 'balancing point' might sit — a quick mental estimation before any formula is named. Collect three or four guesses and note them on the board.

Introduce the balance-point model: the mean is the point where total left-distance equals total right-distance. Students verify this for their three numbers by computing distances from candidate points, then articulate in pairs why shifting the candidate left or right immediately breaks equality. Establish the uniqueness argument through discussion.

Figure it Out Q2, section 5.1 p.113 ("A dot plot shows a collection with its mean of 9 but one dot is missing....") — students mark the missing value using the balance-property rather than the average formula, explaining their reasoning aloud. Move to Figure it Out Q4, section 5.1 p.114 ("Three dot plots show song lengths for different albums...."), where students identify the target album and argue why the others fail the balance test.
Pairs share one sentence each: 'The mean must be unique because…'. Consolidate with a class statement connecting the verbal argument to the arithmetic definition of mean.

periods.teacher_notes: Watch for students who compute the mean numerically rather than reading distances from the dot plot — the goal here is the geometric reasoning, not the formula. Students who conflate 'closest to the middle' with 'balance point' benefit from a counter-example using a highly skewed small dataset. Having established that the mean is a uniquely determined balance point, later units can build on this to reason about how adding or removing values shifts the balance.
materials: Plain paper for hand-drawn number lines

periods.activity_title: How Adding or Removing Values Shifts the Mean

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 5.1 p.114
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the median of a 16-value dataset; then reason about (i) one value that can be added without changing the median, (ii) two values that can be added without changing it, (iii) one value that can be removed without changing it.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 5.1 p.115
textbook_items_in_class.description: Examine four statements about mean/median behaviour (removing a value less than median; including a value less than mean; including 4 values; including 4 values less than median) and classify each as always/sometimes/never true.

time_bands.activity: Present a small dataset (e.g., {3, 5, 7, 9, 11}) on the board. Students compute the mean mentally, then predict aloud: 'If I add 15 to this set, does the mean go up, down, or stay?' Record predictions before revealing the answer.

Guide students to discover the rule: a value above the mean pulls it up; a value below pulls it down; a value equal to the mean leaves it unchanged. Extend to symmetric additions — adding one value above and one equally below the mean — and have students verify by computing the new mean. Groups then predict what happens to the median under the same additions.

Figure it Out Q5, section 5.1 p.114 ("Find the median of a 16-value dataset; then reason about (i) one value that can be added without changing the median....") — students sort the dataset, find the median, and systematically reason about each sub-question. Transition to Figure it Out Q6, section 5.1 p.115 ("Examine four statements about mean/median behaviour...."), classifying statements as always/sometimes/never true and giving one justifying example or counter-example for each.
Each student writes one 'always true' statement about mean or median behaviour in their own words, ready to share. Circulate and flag any that confuse mean and median.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is assuming that removing any value will change both mean and median; students need to discover the counter-example (removing the median value from an odd-count dataset) themselves. Encourage students to test conjectures with a specific small dataset before generalising. The balance-point model established with dot plots provides the geometric ground for these reasoning steps.

periods.activity_title: Proving What Happens When Every Value Shifts or Scales

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Try This, p.107
textbook_items_in_class.description: Students explain algebraically (and using fair-share interpretation) what happens to the average when a fixed number is subtracted from every value, and then investigate what happens when every value is doubled.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 5.1 p.113
textbook_items_in_class.description: Class average height of 24 students is 150.2 cm, measured with shoes adding 1 cm; determine whether remeasurement is needed and compute the correct average height (149.2 cm) from six options.

time_bands.activity: State the proposition: 'If every value in a dataset is increased by a constant c, the mean increases by exactly c.' Ask students whether they believe this is always true or only sometimes, and have them give a gut-response reason.

Walk through the algebraic proof together: write the mean formula for n values, add c to each, factor out, and identify the new mean. Repeat for subtraction. Then work through Try This, p.107 ("Students explain algebraically...what happens to the average when a fixed number is subtracted from every value, and then investigate what happens when every value is doubled.") — students produce the doubling proof in pairs using the distributive property, and connect it to the fair-share interpretation.

Figure it Out Q3, section 5.1 p.113 ("Class average height of 24 students is 150.2 cm, measured with shoes adding 1 cm....") — students apply the proven shift rule to determine the correct average without recomputing individual heights, choosing from the six options and justifying their choice algebraically.
Students write a one-sentence 'proof summary' for each case (shift and scale) in their notebooks, using their own words. Invite two students to read aloud; correct any symbolic errors on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently attempt to verify the shift rule only numerically; push them toward the algebraic argument using sigma notation or the expanded sum, so the generalisation is clear for any n. Watch for errors in the doubling proof where students forget to divide by n after multiplying every term. Figure it Out Q3 is an ideal test of whether they can apply the rule without revisiting raw data.

periods.activity_title: Finding the Unknown Using the Mean Formula

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Finding the Unknown (wrestlers), p.109
textbook_items_in_class.description: Given the mean weight of 10 wrestlers (39.2 kg) and 9 of the 10 weights, uses the mean formula to set up and solve a linear equation to find the missing weight (43 kg).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Finding the Unknown (coconuts), p.109
textbook_items_in_class.description: Given the average coconut harvest per tree (25.6) across 15 trees and the information that one tree's count was recorded 3 more than actual, recovers the total harvest and computes the corrected average (25.4).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 5.1 p.115
textbook_items_in_class.description: The mean of 8 numbers (8, 13, 10, 4, 5, 20, y, 10) is 10.375; find the value of y.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 5.1 p.115
textbook_items_in_class.description: A dataset has 15 values with mean 134; find the sum of the data.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q9, section 5.1 p.115
homework.description: Given 11 values including unknown p and median 29, determine which candidate values of p (10, 25, 40, 100, 29, 47, 30) are consistent with the given median.

time_bands.activity: Read Finding the Unknown (wrestlers), p.109 ("Given the mean weight of 10 wrestlers (39.2 kg) and 9 of the 10 weights....") together. Model setting up the equation: total weight = mean × count, then isolate the unknown. Students copy the equation structure and verify the answer of 43 kg.

Finding the Unknown (coconuts), p.109 ("Given the average coconut harvest per tree (25.6) across 15 trees and the information that one tree's count was recorded 3 more than actual....") — students attempt this in pairs before the teacher reveals the method. Discuss the two-step structure: recover the original total, subtract the overcounting, recompute the corrected mean.

Figure it Out Q7, section 5.1 p.115 ("The mean of 8 numbers...is 10.375; find the value of y.") and Figure it Out Q8, section 5.1 p.115 ("A dataset has 15 values with mean 134; find the sum of the data.") — students solve independently, showing equation set-up and working.
Peer-check: pairs exchange notebooks and verify each other's equations. Highlight the step where mean × count = sum, and flag answers where students divided instead of multiplied.

periods.teacher_notes: The most common error here is inverting the formula — dividing the known sum by an unknown count instead of multiplying mean by count. Insist students write 'sum = mean × count' explicitly before manipulating. Finding the Unknown (coconuts), p.109 is subtler because the overcounting applies to one entry in the total, not to the mean directly; slow groups may benefit from re-reading the problem sentence by sentence.

periods.activity_title: Mean and Median from Frequency Tables

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Mean and Median with Frequencies (family size), p.110
textbook_items_in_class.description: Calculates mean and median of a frequency-table dataset of family sizes for 36 students, demonstrating the weighted-sum formula for mean and the cumulative-frequency method for locating the median position.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q11, section 5.1 p.115
textbook_items_in_class.description: Frequency table shows number of trials to hit a dart bull's-eye for a school competition; describe the data using minimum, maximum, mean, and median.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q10, section 5.1 p.115
textbook_items_in_class.description: Dot plot shows weekly cycle-riding frequency; four students rode twice. Find average, median, evaluate five validity statements about the data, and predict next week's average and median if everyone rode one extra time.

time_bands.activity: Read Mean and Median with Frequencies (family size), p.110 ("Calculates mean and median of a frequency-table dataset of family sizes for 36 students....") together. Emphasise the weighted-sum column (value × frequency) and cumulative-frequency column. Students reproduce the table in their notebooks and confirm the mean and median.

Figure it Out Q11, section 5.1 p.115 ("Frequency table shows number of trials to hit a dart bull's-eye....") — students build the table columns, compute the weighted sum and mean, use cumulative frequency to find the median, then describe the dataset in three sentences covering minimum, maximum, mean, and median.

Figure it Out Q10, section 5.1 p.115 ("Dot plot shows weekly cycle-riding frequency; four students rode twice....") — students read the dot plot, find the average and median, evaluate the five validity statements, and apply the shift-by-one rule (from the algebraic proof that shifting every value by a constant shifts the mean by that constant) to predict next week's statistics.
Quick verbal round: each student names one thing that is the same and one thing that is different when computing the median from raw data versus from a frequency table.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often stop at computing the mean from a frequency table and forget to locate the median position using cumulative frequencies; remind them that the median's position is (n+1)/2 for odd n and between n/2 and n/2+1 for even n, found by scanning the cumulative column. The dot-plot question links the algebraic shift rule to a visual context, reinforcing the earlier proof. For students who finish early, the self-study pointer is Mean and Median with Frequencies (family size), p.110, which they can re-read to note the two-column construction method.

periods.activity_title: Spreadsheets: Cell References and AVERAGE Formulae

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 5.1 p.113
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the mean of (i) first 50 natural numbers, (ii) first 50 odd numbers, (iii) first 50 multiples of 4; share observations.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the spreadsheet layout: rows, columns, cell references (e.g., B3, D2:D6). Show a printed or projected marks table and have students identify which cell holds a specific value, practising the reference notation as a naming game.

Demonstrate (or describe) writing =SUM(B3:G3) and =AVERAGE(B3:G3) for a row of marks. Students then write the corresponding formulae for a column range on paper, predicting the output before a calculator check. Connect =AVERAGE to the weighted-sum formula they computed manually in earlier units, showing that the tool applies the same arithmetic.

Figure it Out Q1, section 5.1 p.113 ("Find the mean of (i) first 50 natural numbers, (ii) first 50 odd numbers, (iii) first 50 multiples of 4; share observations.") — students use the arithmetic-series shortcut (or direct computation) to find each mean, then articulate the pattern: the mean of the first 50 natural numbers equals the mean of a symmetric set around its midpoint. Link: in a spreadsheet, =AVERAGE over the range would yield the same result.
Students write one spreadsheet formula they would use to find the class average on a test, specifying a realistic cell range. Pairs check each other's notation for correct colon syntax.

periods.teacher_notes: Where computers are unavailable, the spreadsheet sub-topic can be taught entirely with pencil-and-paper simulation: students 'become' the spreadsheet by filling in a printed blank table and writing formulae in formula-bar boxes. The risk is students memorising =AVERAGE without connecting it to sum÷count; insist they expand the formula into its arithmetic equivalent at least once. Figure it Out Q1 reveals a beautiful pattern (mean of first n natural numbers = (n+1)/2) that rewards those who look for it.

periods.activity_title: Extended Practice: Mean, Median, and Mixed Problems

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 5.1 p.115
textbook_items_in_class.description: Examine four statements about mean/median behaviour (removing a value less than median; including a value less than mean; including 4 values; including 4 values less than median) and classify each as always/sometimes/never true.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q9, section 5.1 p.115
textbook_items_in_class.description: Given 11 values including unknown p and median 29, determine which candidate values of p (10, 25, 40, 100, 29, 47, 30) are consistent with the given median.

time_bands.activity: Return to Figure it Out Q6, section 5.1 p.115 ("Examine four statements about mean/median behaviour....") — this time students are asked to produce counter-examples for any 'sometimes true' statements identified earlier. Groups of three compare their counter-examples and resolve disagreements through argument, not by appeal to authority.

Figure it Out Q9, section 5.1 p.115 ("Given 11 values including unknown p and median 29, determine which candidate values of p are consistent with the given median.") — students sort the 10 known values, identify the position that will hold the median once p is inserted, and test each candidate systematically. They record 'yes/no' with a one-line reason for each candidate.

Students pose one original problem of their own: they choose a dataset and an unknown, compute the mean or median, and write a 'find the missing value' question for a partner to solve. Partners solve and verify each other's answers.

Whole-class debrief: what makes a 'find the unknown' problem well-posed? Students identify what information must be given (mean/median, count, and all other values) for the unknown to be uniquely determined.

periods.teacher_notes: The candidate-testing approach in Figure it Out Q9 is systematic and prepares students for always/sometimes/never reasoning in more complex contexts. Watch for students who insert p into an unsorted list and read off the wrong position as the median. The problem-posing activity in the third band strengthens ownership of the method and typically surfaces creative edge cases the class has not yet considered.

periods.activity_title: Introducing Line Graphs: Temperature and Launches

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Line Graphs — Temperature (Kerala and Punjab), p.116–118
textbook_items_in_class.description: Demonstrates the two-step identify-then-infer process on a clustered line graph of monthly maximum temperatures (2023), identifying scale, markers, and trends; inferring Punjab's higher variability versus Kerala's near-constant tropical climate.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Line Graphs — Space Launches, p.119–120
textbook_items_in_class.description: Applies the two-step process to a multi-series line graph of annual space-object launches (2012–2024) for USA, China, Russia, and worldwide; distinguishes valid inferences from invalid ones (e.g., cannot infer Nepal launched nothing, cannot read individual year counts precisely from the graph).

time_bands.activity: Ask students: 'When is a line graph better than a bar graph?' Take three answers, then introduce the principle — line graphs suit data that evolves over time, because connected points signal continuity. Students identify the x-axis (time), y-axis (quantity), scale, and colour/marker conventions as a class before reading any values.

Line Graphs — Temperature (Kerala and Punjab), p.116–118 ("Demonstrates the two-step identify-then-infer process on a clustered line graph of monthly maximum temperatures (2023)....") — Step 1: students identify what the graph shows (units, scale, two state lines, year). Step 2: students infer — in pairs — which state shows greater variability, the month of highest temperature for each, and what the near-constant Kerala line implies about its climate. Pairs share inferences; class votes on which are well-supported.

Line Graphs — Space Launches, p.119–120 ("Applies the two-step process to a multi-series line graph of annual space-object launches (2012–2024)....") — students apply the same two-step framework independently: identify all series, then produce two valid and one invalid inference in writing. Class compares invalid inferences and explains why each fails.
Students write the two-step framework as a personal rule in their notebooks: Step 1 (identify — scale, units, series, range) and Step 2 (infer — compare, trend, what the data cannot tell us).

periods.teacher_notes: Students regularly conflate 'the line is high' with 'the rate of change is large'; draw attention to slope as distinct from height. The space-launches graph is particularly good for practising invalid-inference detection — the absence of a country on the chart does not mean it launched nothing. For confident students, Line Graphs — Space Launches, p.119–120 contains a sub-question about reading precise values from a graph that can serve as a self-study extension.
materials: Printed or projected graphs from the textbook
Coloured markers for annotating the graph

periods.activity_title: Rainfall Line Graphs and Monthly-Average Data

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 5.2 p.122
textbook_items_in_class.description: Tabular data of average daily customers visiting vs. purchasing across days of the week; visualise on a line graph.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 5.2 p.122
textbook_items_in_class.description: Average monthly rainfall (days) for Mangaluru, New Delhi, Port Blair, Rameswaram; plot three cities on a given line graph, fill in New Delhi data from the graph, compare rainiest and driest cities, identify rainy seasons.

time_bands.activity: Revisit what 'monthly-average' means: the rainfall data is itself a mean computed over many years. Ask: 'Does this monthly average tell us exactly what will happen in any single year?' Students articulate what the data can and cannot tell — linking directly to the two-step framework's second step.

Figure it Out Q1, section 5.2 p.122 ("Tabular data of average daily customers visiting vs. purchasing across days of the week; visualise on a line graph.") — students choose an appropriate scale, plot both series on a single graph, label axes, and add a legend. Pairs review each other's graphs for scale errors and missing labels.

Figure it Out Q2, section 5.2 p.122 ("Average monthly rainfall (days) for Mangaluru, New Delhi, Port Blair, Rameswaram; plot three cities on a given line graph....") — students plot three of the four cities, read New Delhi data from the partially completed graph, compare rainiest and driest cities, and identify rainy seasons from the multi-series shape.

Students answer in one sentence: 'What does the shape of the Rameswaram line tell us that the table alone does not?' Collect answers verbally; highlight responses that reference rate of change rather than just maximum value.

periods.teacher_notes: Choosing an appropriate y-axis scale is a persistent difficulty — students often start at zero even when all values are large, producing a graph where differences are invisible. Model scale selection explicitly before students begin Figure it Out Q1. The rainfall data introduces the idea that displayed values are themselves averages — a concept that rewards careful reading and prepares students for the infographic unit ahead.

periods.activity_title: Reading a Choropleth Infographic: Rice and Wheat Consumption

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3 (births graph), section 5.2 p.123
textbook_items_in_class.description: Line graph of monthly births in India over a time period; make observations, estimate births in July 2017, identify time period captured, compare January births across 2018–2020, estimate total births in 2019.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the choropleth infographic: a map where colour encodes per-capita rice and wheat consumption across Indian states. Students first spend time simply looking — identifying the colour scale, the two crops, and which regions appear darkest. No inferences yet.

Students record three geographic patterns they observe (e.g., southern states tend toward rice; northern plains toward wheat) and then explicitly label each as 'observation' or 'inference'. Class discussion: what additional information would be needed to move from observation to inference? Discuss one inference the map cannot support and why colour encoding has limits.

Figure it Out Q3 (births graph), section 5.2 p.123 ("Line graph of monthly births in India over a time period; make observations, estimate births in July 2017....") — students apply the two-step framework to a time-series line graph, making observations first, then producing estimates and cross-period comparisons.

Exit question: 'What is one thing a choropleth map shows that a line graph cannot, and vice versa?' Students write one sentence each. Collect to check understanding of the purpose of different representations.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often treat the colour encoding as exact (e.g., 'state X consumes exactly Y kg per capita') when the colour represents a range; emphasise that the map reveals relative patterns, not precise quantities. The births line graph provides a useful contrast: it gives a time dimension that the choropleth lacks, but loses the geographic dimension entirely. Watch for students who estimate from the graph by extrapolating trends rather than reading values within the displayed range.
materials: Printed or projected choropleth map and births graph from textbook

periods.activity_title: Activity Strips: Decoding and Creating Time-Use Representations

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Try This, p.125
textbook_items_in_class.description: Students create their own 48-box activity strip for different days of the week, marking five activity types in 30-minute intervals, and compare their strip with an adult family member's strip.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q12, section 5.2 p.131
homework.description: Individual project: create activity strips for different days of the week; track eating/sleeping regularity and outdoor time; calculate average time per activity; compare with an adult's strip.

time_bands.activity: Present the 48-box strip framework: each box represents one 30-minute interval across a 24-hour day; five colours code five activities. Students decode Manoj's Friday strip from the textbook page, naming the dominant activity for each segment of the day.

Students decode Manoj's Saturday and Sunday strips, then infer which day includes a long movie outing by identifying an unusual unbroken colour block. Groups compare their inferences and resolve disagreements by counting boxes.

Try This, p.125 ("Students create their own 48-box activity strip for different days of the week, marking five activity types in 30-minute intervals....") — each student draws a blank 48-box strip for their own yesterday, colours it in, and computes the total time per activity by counting boxes (each box = 0.5 hours). Students write two observations about their own strip.

Pairs compare strips: which activities align between the two students? Which diverge most? Students frame one comparison as a data statement ('On weekdays, I spend ___ hours on ___, while my partner spends ___ hours'). Assign Figure it Out Q12, section 5.2 p.131 ("Individual project: create activity strips for different days of the week....") as homework.

periods.teacher_notes: The 48-box strip is a novel representation — confirm students understand that the 48 boxes are sequential (box 1 = midnight to 12:30 am) before they decode Manoj's strips. A common error is treating the strip as a pie chart (proportional area) rather than a sequential timeline; the order of the boxes carries meaning. The homework project extends the single-day strip to multiple days, introducing temporal comparison.
materials: Printed 48-box strip templates or squared paper

periods.activity_title: Sleep-Duration Curve and Smooth-Curve Line Graphs

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q10, section 5.2 p.130
textbook_items_in_class.description: Line graph on primary lighting source (kerosene vs electricity) in rural/urban India 1983–2023; evaluate four validity statements.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q11, section 5.2 p.130
textbook_items_in_class.description: Line graph of daily time spent on hobbies and games by rural/urban children by age; answer two read-off questions and evaluate two interpretive statements.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the sleep-duration curve from the textbook: a line graph of average daily sleep from age 6 to 75 with approximately 70 data points. Ask students: 'Why is this plotted as a smooth curve rather than 70 separate bars?' Students propose reasons, then the teacher consolidates: when data points are dense and ordered by age, a connected curve reveals the trend more clearly than columns would.

Students identify the key features of the sleep curve: where it decreases (adolescence), where it is lowest (mid-adulthood), and where it rises again (after age 50). They write two 'valid' and one 'invalid' inference about the curve, applying the two-step framework.

Figure it Out Q10, section 5.2 p.130 ("Line graph on primary lighting source (kerosene vs electricity) in rural/urban India 1983–2023; evaluate four validity statements.") and Figure it Out Q11, section 5.2 p.130 ("Line graph of daily time spent on hobbies and games by rural/urban children by age....") — students evaluate the validity statements for each graph, writing one-sentence justifications.

Class debrief: collect one 'always invalid' inference type the class has noticed across multiple graphs (e.g., inferring exact values from a smooth curve; inferring causation from correlation). Students add this to their two-step framework notes.

periods.teacher_notes: The distinction between a smooth curve (many closely spaced data points) and a bar graph (discrete categories) is conceptually important — help students see that the choice of representation follows the nature of the data. In Figure it Out Q10, the crossing of the kerosene and electricity lines is a powerful visual event; ask students to identify the approximate year it occurred and what it implies. A self-study pointer for confident students: Try This, p.131 (moonrise/moonset) — see Figure it Out Q15, section 5.2 p.132.
materials: Printed or projected sleep-duration curve and Q10, Q11 graphs

periods.activity_title: Plotting and Comparing Multi-Series Line Graphs

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q9, section 5.2 p.129
textbook_items_in_class.description: Retail price of iodised salt (INR) across 6 states from 2016–2025: (i) plot 3 states on a line graph; (ii) share observations; (iii) compare Gujarat and Uttar Pradesh; (iv) find the state with the greatest price increase; (v) explore further.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 5.2 p.128
textbook_items_in_class.description: Average weight was 65.3 kg, median 67 kg; one person lost 2 kg and two gained 1 kg each — predict what happens to mean and median this month.

time_bands.activity: Figure it Out Q9, section 5.2 p.129 ("Retail price of iodised salt (INR) across 6 states from 2016–2025: (i) plot 3 states on a line graph....") — students select three states, set a scale, plot the series with distinct markers, and add a legend. Partners check each other's axes and legend labels.

Continue Figure it Out Q9: students share two observations from their graph, then compare Gujarat and Uttar Pradesh in writing, and identify the state with the greatest total price increase by computing the difference between the 2025 and 2016 values from the data table.

Figure it Out Q8, section 5.2 p.128 ("Average weight was 65.3 kg, median 67 kg; one person lost 2 kg and two gained 1 kg each — predict what happens to mean and median this month.") — students apply the balance-point reasoning developed in the balance-act units: net change in sum = −2 + 1 + 1 = 0, so the mean is unchanged; then reason carefully about whether the median shifts based on each person's weight relative to 67 kg.
Students summarise Figure it Out Q8 in two sentences: one for the mean prediction and one for the median prediction, with a brief algebraic justification for each.

periods.teacher_notes: Figure it Out Q8 deliberately bridges the two sections of the chapter — it applies balance-point and shift reasoning to a real scenario — so students who connect the net-change calculation to the mean formula are demonstrating the deepest understanding. In Figure it Out Q9, watch for students who judge 'greatest increase' by the highest current price rather than by computing the absolute change over the period.

periods.activity_title: Mean Grids, Median Constraints, and Algebraic Mean Puzzles

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 5.2 p.127
textbook_items_in_class.description: Mean grids: (i) fill a 3×3 grid with 9 distinct numbers so each row, column, and diagonal averages 10; (ii) vary numbers while preserving the average in all directions.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 5.2 p.127
textbook_items_in_class.description: Give two examples each for: (i) 3 numbers with mean 8; (ii) 4 numbers with median 15.5; (iii) 5 numbers with mean 13.6; (iv) 6 numbers where mean = median; (v) 6 numbers where mean > median.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 5.2 p.127
textbook_items_in_class.description: Fill three blanks in the collection (5, 21, 14, _, _, _) so its median is 13; count how many possibilities exist for counting numbers.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 5.2 p.127
textbook_items_in_class.description: Fill two blanks in (3, 11, _, _, 15, 6) so its mean is 6.5; count possibilities for counting numbers.

time_bands.activity: Figure it Out Q1, section 5.2 p.127 ("Mean grids: (i) fill a 3×3 grid with 9 distinct numbers so each row, column, and diagonal averages 10....") — students attempt part (i) individually, then compare strategies in pairs. Discuss: why must the centre cell equal the overall mean? Extend by having students vary three cells while preserving the row-column-diagonal average.

Figure it Out Q2, section 5.2 p.127 ("Give two examples each for: (i) 3 numbers with mean 8; (ii) 4 numbers with median 15.5....") — students work through all five sub-questions, emphasising that the case 'mean = median' requires deliberate construction and 'mean > median' requires a right-skewed distribution.

Figure it Out Q3, section 5.2 p.127 ("Fill three blanks in (5, 21, 14, _, _, _) so its median is 13....") and Figure it Out Q4, section 5.2 p.127 ("Fill two blanks in (3, 11, _, _, 15, 6) so its mean is 6.5....") — students solve each, then count possibilities by considering the positional constraints systematically.

Students share the most surprising valid example from Figure it Out Q2 and explain why it is non-obvious. Highlight the case where mean > median and ask: 'What does this tell us about the shape of the dataset?'

periods.teacher_notes: The mean grid is a rich puzzle that rewards students who notice the magic-square structure; the centre-equals-mean insight follows from the fact that every row, column, and diagonal includes the centre, so if all six lines average to the same value, the centre must carry that value. Figure it Out Q3 and Q4 are counting problems as well as statistics problems — students who have found one solution should be pushed to find a second and a third before counting the full set. A self-study pointer: Figure it Out Q5, section 5.2 p.127 ("Check whether each statement is true with algebraic justification....") connects these counting exercises to the algebraic structure of means.

time_bands.activity: Pose a synthesis question: 'A dataset's mean is 17. Every value is doubled. A new value of 34 is then added. What is the new mean?' Students solve in writing, explicitly naming the two algebraic rules they use (scaling scales the mean; adding a value equal to the mean leaves it unchanged). Share reasoning aloud.

Figure it Out Q7, section 5.2 p.128 ("Dot plot of data near 14–23; determine whether 17 is the mean, sharing the method used.") — students choose between computing the arithmetic mean and using the balance-point distance method, justify their choice, and compare the two methods with a partner. Highlight that both routes reach the same answer, demonstrating the equivalence of geometric and algebraic views of the mean.

Figure it Out Q14, section 5.2 p.131 ("Four line graphs show sunrise and sunset times across the year at 4 Indian locations; identify sunrise vs sunset lines, find earliest January sunrise, find location with longest day, share observations.") — students apply the full two-step framework across four simultaneous graphs, drawing comparisons across locations. Students write two observations that connect the statistical pattern (what the graph shows) to a geographic or physical explanation (what it might mean).

Closing reflection: students write three sentences in their notebooks — one connecting the balance-point model to the algebraic mean formula, one describing when a line graph is the right choice and when a different representation works better, and one question they still have about data and its interpretation. Collect the question slips as a teacher's formative gauge.

periods.teacher_notes: The opening synthesis question is designed to chain three results (scaling, shift, adding a value equal to the mean) so students must recall and sequence them; a class that handles it confidently has genuinely internalised the algebraic structure of mean. Figure it Out Q14's four-graph panel rewards students who read across panels rather than within a single graph — push them to identify which location has the greatest annual range of daylight, connecting to the idea of variability explored with the temperature data in the visualising-and-interpreting-data section. items.prompt: A set of five values has a mean of 12. A student claims that if the value 12 is removed from the set, the mean of the remaining four values will still be 12. Is the student correct? Justify your answer using the balance-point model of the mean.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The student is correct. The mean is the balance point where total left-distance equals total right-distance. The value 12 sits exactly at the balance point, contributing zero to either side's distance total. Removing it does not disturb the equality of distances, so the balance point — and hence the mean — of the remaining four values is still 12. Algebraically: original sum = 5 × 12 = 60; removing 12 gives a new sum of 48 and a new count of 4; new mean = 48 ÷ 4 = 12.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the balance-point property: a value equal to the mean contributes zero net distance, so removing it leaves the mean unchanged.

inclusivity.support: Try it with a small concrete set, such as {10, 12, 14}, before generalising.
inclusivity.challenge: What if two values equal to the mean are removed — does the mean still stay the same? Construct an argument.

items.prompt: A sorted dataset of 10 values has a median of 7. A student wants to add two new values to the dataset without changing its median. She proposes adding 3 and 11. Will this preserve the median? Explain your reasoning by referring to how the median is determined for an even-count dataset.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: After adding 3 and 11, the dataset has 12 values. The median of a 12-value sorted dataset is the mean of the 6th and 7th values. Originally, the median of the 10-value set was the mean of the 5th and 6th values, equal to 7. Adding 3 (which is below the median) shifts all values from the 5th position onward one place to the right, and adding 11 (which is above the median) does the same from the opposite end. The 6th and 7th values of the new sorted 12-value set are the same pair whose mean was 7, so the median is preserved. The key reasoning step is that one value below and one above the current median, when inserted, push the two middle values outward by one position each but do not change which values occupy the median positions.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Track the median-position indices after insertion: symmetric additions (one below, one above the median) preserve the values at the new median positions.

inclusivity.support: Write out a specific 10-value set with median 7, insert 3 and 11, sort, and count to the 6th and 7th positions.
inclusivity.challenge: Find a pair of additions that are NOT symmetric around 7 yet still preserve the median, and explain why.

items.prompt: Every value in a dataset is increased by 5. A student says the mean increases by 5 but the median stays the same. Is each part of this claim correct or incorrect? Provide a clear algebraic argument for your answer about the mean, and a sorting-based argument for your answer about the median.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The mean claim is correct and the median claim is incorrect. For the mean: if the original values are x₁, x₂, …, xₙ with mean M = (x₁ + x₂ + … + xₙ)/n, then after adding 5 to each value the new mean is (x₁+5 + x₂+5 + … + xₙ+5)/n = (x₁ + … + xₙ)/n + 5n/n = M + 5. So the mean increases by exactly 5. For the median: adding 5 to every value preserves the sorted order (since adding the same constant to all values does not change their relative order), and the value in the middle position is now 5 more than before. So the median also increases by exactly 5. The student's claim about the median is incorrect.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the distributive property for the mean proof, and the order-preservation argument for the median proof.

inclusivity.support: Talk through your reasoning with a partner before writing, using the set {2, 4, 6, 8, 10} as a concrete example.
inclusivity.challenge: What if only some values are increased by 5, not all — construct a case where the mean increases by less than 5 and the median stays the same.

items.prompt: The mean of six numbers is 14. Five of the numbers are 8, 11, 17, 20, and 12. Find the sixth number. Show your working using the mean formula.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Sum of all six numbers = mean × count = 14 × 6 = 84. Sum of the five known numbers = 8 + 11 + 17 + 20 + 12 = 68. Sixth number = 84 − 68 = 16.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use sum = mean × count to find the total, then subtract the sum of known values.

inclusivity.support: Sketch a number line and place the five known values; the mean of 14 is the balance point — estimate where the sixth value should be before computing.
inclusivity.challenge: If the sixth number were changed so that the mean becomes 15, what would the new sixth number be?

items.prompt:
A frequency table shows the number of books read by students in a month:

| Books read | Frequency |
|---|---|
| 1 | 4 |
| 2 | 7 |
| 3 | 5 |
| 4 | 4 |

Find the mean and median number of books read. Show your working.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Total students = 4 + 7 + 5 + 4 = 20. Weighted sum = (1×4) + (2×7) + (3×5) + (4×4) = 4 + 14 + 15 + 16 = 49. Mean = 49 ÷ 20 = 2.45 books. Cumulative frequencies: 4, 11, 16, 20. The median is the mean of the 10th and 11th values. The 10th value falls in the group 'books read = 2' (cumulative reaches 11 at books = 2, and 4 at books = 1, so positions 5–11 are books = 2). The 11th value is also in the group 'books read = 2'. Median = (2 + 2) ÷ 2 = 2 books.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the weighted-sum formula for the mean and cumulative frequencies to locate the median position.

inclusivity.support: Fill in the cumulative frequency column first, then locate which group contains position 10 and which contains position 11.
inclusivity.challenge: If two more students who each read 4 books join the group, by how much does the mean change? Show with the formula.

items.prompt: The mean of the first 50 odd numbers is:

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 50. The first 50 odd numbers are 1, 3, 5, …, 99. Their sum = 50² = 2500. Mean = 2500 ÷ 50 = 50. Alternatively, the first and last values are 1 and 99; for an arithmetic sequence, mean = (first + last)/2 = (1 + 99)/2 = 50.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the arithmetic-sequence mean formula: mean = (first term + last term) ÷ 2, or sum = n² for the first n odd numbers.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student likely computed the mean of the first 50 natural numbers (mean = 25.5, rounded to 25) rather than the first 50 odd numbers.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may have found the 50th odd number (99) and divided by a wrong count, or confused the last term with the mean plus one.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may have subtracted 1 from the correct answer, possibly confusing the mean with the last term minus something.

inclusivity.support: List the first five odd numbers, compute their mean, and look for a pattern before tackling 50 numbers.
inclusivity.challenge: Without computing, predict the mean of the first 100 odd numbers and justify your prediction using the pattern.

items.prompt: A class of 20 students has an average score of 72 on a test. The teacher discovers that one student's score of 60 was recorded as 80 by mistake. What is the corrected average? Show your method.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Original total = 72 × 20 = 1440. The recorded score of 80 should be 60, so the actual total = 1440 − 80 + 60 = 1420. Corrected mean = 1420 ÷ 20 = 71. Alternatively: the overcount is 20, so the mean decreases by 20 ÷ 20 = 1, giving 72 − 1 = 71.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find the original sum, apply the correction to the sum, then divide by the count.

inclusivity.support: Write out the two steps separately: first find the original total, then adjust it for the recording error.
inclusivity.challenge: Two students' scores were each recorded 5 marks too high. By how much does the mean change? Generalise for k students each overcounted by d marks.

items.prompt: A line graph shows the monthly maximum temperature (°C) for two cities, City P and City Q, over one year. City P's line stays between 28 °C and 32 °C throughout the year. City Q's line rises from 18 °C in January to 42 °C in May, then falls back to 20 °C in December. Write two valid inferences and one statement that the graph does NOT support, explaining briefly why each is or is not supported.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Valid inference 1: City Q has much greater monthly temperature variability than City P, since its line spans a range of 24 °C compared to City P's range of only 4 °C. Valid inference 2: City Q's maximum temperature is highest in May. Statement the graph does not support (example): 'City P is closer to the equator than City Q' — the graph shows temperature values only; geographic location cannot be inferred from a temperature graph alone. Any inference about cause (climate type, geographic position) is not directly supported by the graph, only the patterns within the data are.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the two-step framework: identify what the graph shows (scale, range, both series), then distinguish data-supported patterns from inferences that require additional information.

inclusivity.support: Use a visual representation — sketch the two lines roughly — before writing the inferences.
inclusivity.challenge: What additional graph or data source would you need to support the claim that City P is located near the equator? Explain.

The table below shows the average number of customers visiting and purchasing at a stall each day.

|---|---|---|

| Tuesday | 55 | 22 |
| Wednesday | 30 | 10 |
| Thursday | 60 | 27 |

items.visual_stimulus:
| Day | Visitors | Buyers |
|---|---|---|
| Monday | 40 | 18 |
| Tuesday | 55 | 22 |
| Wednesday | 30 | 10 |
| Thursday | 60 | 27 |
| Friday | 75 | 35 |

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (i) Compute buyer-to-visitor ratios: Monday 18/40 = 0.45; Tuesday 22/55 = 0.40; Wednesday 10/30 = 0.333; Thursday 27/60 = 0.45; Friday 35/75 = 0.467. Highest ratio is Friday (≈ 0.467). (ii) Total visitors = 40 + 55 + 30 + 60 + 75 = 260. Mean visitors = 260 ÷ 5 = 52.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compute the ratio for each day to answer (i); apply sum ÷ count to answer (ii).

items.prompt: A 48-box activity strip represents one full day in 30-minute intervals. Colour code: Blue = sleep, Green = school, Yellow = meals, Red = outdoor play, White = screen time. Riya's strip shows 16 blue boxes, 10 green boxes, 6 yellow boxes, 4 red boxes, and 12 white boxes. (i) How many hours does Riya spend on screen time? (ii) What fraction of the day is spent sleeping?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (i) 12 white boxes × 30 minutes = 360 minutes = 6 hours of screen time. (ii) 16 blue boxes × 30 minutes = 480 minutes = 8 hours sleeping. Fraction of day = 8/24 = 1/3.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply box count by 30 minutes per box to convert to hours; express sleep hours as a fraction of 24.

items.prompt: A line graph of rural electricity access (%) in India from 1983 to 2023 shows the value rising steeply from 1983 to 2020 and then levelling off near 100%. Which of the following is a valid inference from this graph?

options.label: A
options.text: Rural electricity access increased every single year without exception between 1983 and 2023.

options.label: B
options.text: The rate of increase in rural electricity access was greater in the period 2000–2020 than in 1983–2000, as shown by the steeper rise visible in the graph.

options.label: C
options.text: By 2023, every rural household in India had access to electricity.

options.label: D
options.text: Kerosene use in rural India fell to zero by 2023 because electricity access rose to nearly 100%.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Option B. The graph shows a steeper slope in the 2000–2020 period compared to 1983–2000, making the comparative rate-of-increase statement a valid inference directly supported by the shape of the line. The other options make claims the graph cannot support: year-by-year continuity cannot be read from a line graph (A); 'nearly 100%' on the graph does not mean every household (C); a different fuel's behaviour cannot be inferred from an electricity graph alone (D).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the two-step framework: identify what the graph directly shows (% access over time), then evaluate each statement against what the graph can and cannot tell.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student confuses 'the line is increasing overall' with 'it increased every single year' — a line graph's smooth appearance does not guarantee monotone increase at every point.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student conflates 'access rate near 100%' with 'every household has access' — a percentage near 100 still leaves a non-zero group without access.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student makes a causal inference about a different variable (kerosene) from a graph that only shows electricity access — a classic over-reading of the data.

inclusivity.support: For each option, ask: does the graph literally show this, or am I adding information the graph does not contain?
inclusivity.challenge: Sketch what the kerosene-use graph might look like if it were shown alongside this electricity graph, and identify one further inference that would then become valid.

items.prompt: The retail price of iodised salt (in INR per kg) in a state was ₹12 in 2016 and ₹20 in 2025. (i) What is the total increase in price over this period? (ii) If prices increased by the same amount each year from 2016 to 2025 (9 equal steps), what would be the price in 2020? Show your working.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (i) Total increase = 20 − 12 = ₹8. (ii) There are 9 steps from 2016 to 2025. Annual increase = 8 ÷ 9 ≈ 0.889 INR per year. From 2016 to 2020 is 4 steps. Price in 2020 = 12 + 4 × (8/9) = 12 + 32/9 = 12 + 3.556 ≈ ₹15.56. Accept any correctly rounded answer between ₹15.5 and ₹15.6.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compute the equal annual increment (total change ÷ number of steps) and add the appropriate number of increments to the starting value.

inclusivity.support: Draw a number line from 2016 to 2025 and mark the two known prices; then divide the gap into equal parts before computing.
inclusivity.challenge: If the price had instead grown by the same percentage each year (compound growth), would the 2020 price be higher or lower than under equal annual increments? Explain without computing.

items.prompt: Fill a 3 × 3 grid with nine distinct whole numbers so that every row, every column, and both diagonals have the same mean. The centre cell must be 10. Find one valid set of nine numbers and verify that each row, column, and diagonal averages to 10.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: One valid solution: place 10 in the centre. Choose eight other distinct whole numbers symmetric around 10, for example: top row 7, 12, 11; middle row 13, 10, 7 — but all nine must be distinct. A standard symmetric solution: {2, 14, 10} in one row, {12, 10, 8} in another, {16, 6, 18} — adjust to keep all distinct. A clean example: Row 1: 6, 14, 10; Row 2: 16, 10, 4; Row 3: 8, 6, 16 — check for distinctness and adjust. Simplest valid example using the magic-square structure offset to centre at 10: take the standard 3×3 magic square (centre 5, sum 15 per row) and add 5 to every cell to get centre 10, row/column/diagonal sum 30, mean 10. Numbers: 6, 11, 7 (row 1); 9, 10, 11 — conflict. Use standard magic square: 2 7 6 / 9 5 1 / 4 3 8, add 5: 7 12 11 / 14 10 6 / 9 8 13. Row sums: 30, 30, 30. Column sums: 30, 30, 30. Diagonals: 7+10+13=30, 11+10+9=30. Mean per line = 10. All nine numbers (6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14) are distinct.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Shift the standard 3×3 magic square (centre 5) by adding 5 to every cell so the centre becomes 10 and every line sums to 30, giving mean 10.

inclusivity.support: Start by placing 10 in the centre, then try to place two numbers that add up to 20 in any row alongside it.
inclusivity.challenge: Find a second valid grid that is not simply a rotation or reflection of your first solution, and prove it satisfies the conditions.

items.prompt: The average of two numbers is 9. Both numbers are multiples of 3. Which statement is definitely true?

options.label: B
options.text: The average of the two numbers is a multiple of 3.

options.label: C
options.text: The sum of the two numbers is 27.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Option B. The average is 9, which is a multiple of 3. This is always true by the algebraic argument: if both numbers are 3a and 3b, their average is 3(a+b)/2; for the average to be 9, we need a+b = 6, so average = 9 = 3×3, a multiple of 3. Option A is not necessarily true (e.g., 6 and 12). Option C gives a sum of 27, but sum = 2×9 = 18, not 27. Option D is false (e.g., 6 and 12: 6 < 9).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the algebraic form: let the two multiples of 3 be 3a and 3b; their average = 3(a+b)/2; if this equals 9, average = 9 = 3 × 3, confirming it is a multiple of 3.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student assumes the only way for two numbers to average 9 is if both equal 9 — a failure to consider symmetric pairs like (6, 12).
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student computes sum as mean × 3 instead of mean × 2 (count), confusing the number of values with the mean itself.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student assumes both values must exceed the mean, not realising the mean sits between values (one can be below, one above).

inclusivity.support: List two pairs of multiples of 3 that average to 9 before choosing your answer.
inclusivity.challenge: Is the average of any two multiples of 3 always a multiple of 3? Prove it algebraically or find a counter-example.

exercise.description: Check whether each statement is true (with algebraic justification): (i) average of two even numbers is even; (ii) average of any two multiples of 5 is a multiple of 5; (iii) average of any 5 multiples of 5 is a multiple of 5.

items.prompt: A dot plot displays 12 values, all between 14 and 23. A student claims the mean is 17. Describe two different methods you could use to check whether 17 is the mean without computing the full arithmetic average from scratch, and state what you would look for in each method.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Method 1 (balance-point method): treat 17 as the candidate balance point. For each value, compute its distance from 17 (positive if above, negative if below). Sum the positive distances and the negative distances separately. If both sums are equal, 17 is the mean. Method 2 (sum shortcut): compute the sum of deviations from 17 (i.e., add up (each value − 17) for all 12 values). If this total deviation equals zero, 17 is the mean, because the mean is the unique value from which deviations sum to zero.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the balance-point property (total distance above = total distance below) and the zero-deviation property (sum of (x − candidate) = 0 when candidate = mean).

inclusivity.support: Use a number line: mark 17 and place each dot value on it, then measure its distance from 17 on each side.
inclusivity.challenge: If the student's claim is wrong and the actual mean is 18, by how much does the total deviation from 17 differ from zero? Generalise.

items.prompt: A line graph shows the time of moonrise (in hours after midnight) over 30 consecutive days. On day 1 moonrise is at 6:00 am; the moonrise time increases by roughly 50 minutes each day. On which approximate day of the month would moonrise occur at midnight (i.e., 0 hours after midnight or 24 hours after the previous midnight), and what astronomical event does this correspond to? Show your estimation.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Starting at 6:00 am (6 hours after midnight) on day 1 and increasing by approximately 50 minutes (≈ 0.833 hours) per day: to reach 24 hours after midnight (i.e., the next midnight), moonrise must advance by 24 − 6 = 18 hours from day 1. Number of days needed = 18 ÷ 0.833 ≈ 21.6 days. So moonrise occurs near midnight on approximately day 22 or 23 of the month. This corresponds to the full moon (purnima) — when the moon rises near sunset/midnight and is visible all night — or more precisely to the new moon (amavasya), when moonrise and sunrise coincide (around 6 am) and moonset occurs around sunset; the day when moonrise is at midnight is typically near the full moon. Accept day 22–23 with correct reasoning. The astronomical event is purnima (full moon).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Estimate the number of days needed to advance moonrise by 18 hours at 50 minutes per day, and connect the midnight moonrise to the full-moon phase.

inclusivity.support: Use a number line of hours (0 to 24) and mark each day's moonrise at 50-minute intervals, counting up to 24 hours.
inclusivity.challenge: If moonrise advances by 50 minutes per day, after how many days does it complete a full 24-hour cycle and return to 6:00 am? What astronomical cycle does this represent?
